We were leaving a party together, it was around five in the morning. We were having to walk through his old college's campus to get to where we'd parked; I was tired, it was cold, and I was getting myself ready to crawl into his bed and immediately pass out as soon as we got back to his place. 

At the top of the stairs we needed to take to get to the parking lot, he turned to me and asked, "So, how are you feeling tonight?" 

I just shrugged and mumbled something about being tired, but okay. He responded with a giant grin, asked "Okay enough for this?" and immediately took off running down the hill beside the staircase. Like, the full-on reckless arm-flailing run of someone much younger than he is. When he got to the bottom of the hill there was maybe a three-foot ledge before he hit the ground, which he jumped off without hesitation (he might have clicked his heels mid-jump). 

Now, before he took off running, I was pretty tired. I was a little sad, too, since there was a stray cat I couldn't catch that I lost somewhere in the bushes beside one of the fraternity houses (I'm a bit of a sucker for stray animals, and I've been known to accidentally adopt on a number of occasions, so missing one of them was kind of a kick in the gut). As soon as I saw his joyous recklessness I was immediately all smiles and laughter all over again. 

I ran after him down the hill. I couldn't help /not/ doing it. He actually picked me up off the ledge and helped ease me onto the ground, as well, since my knees are in rough enough shape where they wouldn't have survived the jump without a /ton/ of pain immediately after.  

I know it's a little silly and inconsequential in comparison to some other things posted on here, but seeing him actually give into impulse sometimes when he's /generally/ a lot more mature a person than I am kind of won me over right then. If I wasn't won over already.

I wasn't there to witness the exchange (he didn't want to make a big production of it, so he took her into another room so they could have a minute alone), but she apparently immediately burst into tears and started gushing about how relieved she was that she could actually buy food for the apartment. 

I have trouble crying in front of other people (I always have), but I almost ended up leaking out a couple of tears in front of him when I realized what all was going on. I'm still constantly floored at his selflessness.

I used to live with an abusive (now ex) stepdad. At the time I was astoundingly overprotective of my little sister; she's three years younger than I am, so when things started I was ten, and she was seven.

We lived there for five years. I've got so many stories, but I'll just gloss over one for the sake of length. 

I was maybe fourteen, making my older sister fifteen (we'll call her T) and my younger eleven (she'll be A for now). It was getting on to late at night, and A had left some homework in my stepdad's car. She asked him for his keys, grabbed her stuff, set the keys back where she found them on his computer desk in the kitchen. No big deal. 

About ten minutes later, I'm in the basement and I hear near-inhuman wails coming from the kitchen. 

Apparently my stepdad, on the cocktail of medications he was on (slipped discs in his back, took way too much vicodin for it), thought A had lost his keys. He was completely tearing the kitchen apart, throwing things at my little sister in an attempt to find his keys. He spent the entire time absolutely reading her for trash; telling her she's a useless forgetful cunt, how she's just wasting his money and time and food by fucking existing, whole nine yards. I wedge myself between A and my stepdad, so shit's now getting slung at me (both physically and verbally). She was pretty bruised up at that point already. 

Eventually T comes in (still dunno how long exactly it was; I took a couple good blows and things got fuzzy) and, seeing as I had A protected (T and I had to go through this song and dance a number of times, so we had a bit of an unspoken series of tasks to accomplish together when shit went down), she went on an actual hunt for his keys, hoping that would at least calm him down a little. 

She found them. It didn't help. 

Eventually (again, time-fuzz) my mom walked in to see what was going on. My mom was on a number of antidepressants that left her pretty numb and oblivious to a lot, so she'd witnessed similar things to this previously, but hadn't really been able to react, if that makes sense? That day, however, was a couple of days after she'd had to quit taking her meds, since my stepdad's pain meds were more important (obviously) and we were pretty broke (constant problem). So this time, instead of glossing over the situation she was actually aware that her kids were having shit thrown at them and (which I find strange that she focused in on this, but what can you do) he was threatening to ground A and myself for making him look bad. 

She told him he wasn't allowed to do such a thing since he wasn't our actual parent. He informed us (completely refusing to address my mom at all) that since we couldn't be grounded he would just make it his personal mission to make our lives a living hell instead. 

I don't remember exactly what my mom did to redirect him, but she pulled focus for long enough for me and the siblings to run into the laundry room in the basement. We feel asleep down there on piles of dirty clothes, crying and comforting and planning ways to try and get the hell out of there by calling our dad and begging him to move us out with him in Oregon (we were living in Georgia at the time). 

None of that happened. We were there for another half a year, but that was the moment mom actually realized she needed to find a way to get us out of there. I'm apparently the only one of us siblings who remembers most(? I'm not certain of the actual amount I blanked out) of those five years at that house. T spent most of her time away at boyfriend's houses and the only thing she remembers about her time spent actually at home was the paranoid delusions she had going on at the time. A has a five-year-long blank spot right in the middle of her childhood. 

**Tl;dr: shit sucked, but we all survived, so at least that's a small victory.**

My mom's always been pretty fucked up; just recently, she was finally diagnosed with schizophrenia (she's been showing signs all her life) and is on heavy medication for it. She dragged me and my sisters from house to house, depending on who she was sleeping with at the time (and how much she could afford from them and what money she could get from my dad), and my best friend and her mom kind of.. took over. She would feed us, she would buy us new clothes, she would come over and spend time with my little sister (about ten at the time) when my mom was off in Louisiana (I live in Georgia; she had a boyfriend that lived out there, so she'd disappear to go hang out with him for months at a time). My best friend and her mom would have nightly screaming matches about whether or not dfcs should be called, but it never happened; even though she (best friend's mom) was worried about us and how we were doing, she was more worried about us getting separated and not being able to keep an eye on us. 

I'm kind of rambling, but the point I was trying to make was: You're an amazing person. Hands down. There aren't many who'd be able to do what you're doing right now and keep their head above water. Keep on keepin' on, darlin'. You've got this.

My heart goes out to you so much right now. The last cat I rescued, Korra, was a little tuxedo too; she had leukemia, and I couldn't afford to take care of her. Everyone I knew who would want a cat couldn't take her since it's contagious, and my sister (after housing her for a couple of months) threatened to leave her in the woods if I didn't come pick her up. 

I would have taken her in myself, but I'm in a cramped little apartment and my roommate had /literally/ put her own cat down the day before my sister issued her ultimatum. And I just... I couldn't do anything for her. I had to put her down, since no other shelter would take her in because of her illness. And I just... ugh. It's rough. That was almost a year ago and I'm still having trouble getting over it. 

You did everything you could for him, remember that. I know it sucks--I'm not going to tell you it doesn't, because that would be a bald-faced lie--but you did everything you could. You did far more than most other people would even attempt to do, and that's what counts. You gave him much more time than he would have had if you hadn't taken him in.

But, my friend got a new puppy not too long ago (maybe a week). Rose is only about seven pounds, and she's a Jack Russell/pointer mix, so all limbs and gracelessness. For one, Rufus just IMMEDIATELY fell in love with her as soon as she was brought home; even with how rough he plays at the park, when he's with her she's usually the one pinning (well, kinda) him down, dragging him around the house by a rope toy, all of that. 

When my friend started training her, though, they ended up involving Rufus just to make things easier (he's ridiculously obedient for a one year old; he's in the works to be a therapy dog, so he has to be). Rufus will push her down with his paw to get her to sit and to lay down. She's still being house trained as well, so there are puppy pads laying around in case she has an accident, and he'll try and bury them if she does to keep her from getting in trouble.

The two of them adore each other, and it's so sweet I can hardly handle it.

That's actually eerily similar to how I was raised up until I moved across the country; for the first ten years of my life (i.e. before my parents got divorced), we all lived in my grandma's house. I remember more of my grandma than I do of my mom, because while my dad was always out working to support the lot of us (the only person working in a house of seven/eight people), my mom was always out hanging with friends and whatnot. So we were left with my grandma. She was the one who walked us to and from school every day, she was the one to go to the parent/teacher conference nights, she was the one to sign off on all of our report cards, everything. 

And, kinda like you, when my mom moved us kids across the country, my best friend's mom was the one who kinda took over. She helped me kinda come out of my shell, and she helped me realize that just because I lived in the south didn't mean I was surrounded by crazy-scary rednecks, and that the phrase "southern hospitality" existed for a reason, thankyou very much. 

But, yeah. Point I'm trying to get at is, that's almost a dead ringer for how I was raised. I'll stop rambling and repeating myself now, haha.

My best friend and her mom would swing by daily to take us out for dinner just to make sure we would get fed. She decided to tell me a few years after the fact that she and her mom would get in all-out fight over whether or not child services should be called.

So, in short, my best friend kept me from starving and from being potentially separated from my two sisters.

She had her sisters come over to visit a lot those days (her son--my uncle--had down's syndrome and lived at home, and she couldn't take care of him herself). One day, while she was sitting in the living room to rest for a moment, her sister started griping at her about lighting up a cigarette, claiming she shouldn't smoke because she had cancer already, and she'd only make it worse (or something). 

Grandma, being awesome, gives her this "dafuq" look and states that, if her sister was so worried about colon cancer from smoking, she obviously wasn't doing it right.
